analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans that cover other prescription drugs to also cover prescription contraceptives.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill requiring insurance coverage of prescription contraception drew 144 House cosponsors but never received a vote in either committee before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the laws governing employer health plans and health insurance so that any plan covering other prescription drugs or outpatient services could not exclude FDA-approved prescription contraceptives or contraceptive services. It also barred insurers from denying enrollment because of someone's use of contraception, and from penalizing doctors for prescribing it. Women of childbearing age who rely on private insurance would have gained coverage for birth control comparable to what their plans already provide for other drugs and care.
analysis.who_benefits: Women and families with employer-sponsored or individual private insurance, especially the roughly three-quarters of women of childbearing age who rely on such coverage; the bill's findings note women of reproductive age spend 68% more out of pocket on health care than men, largely because of contraception and reproductive care, and that half of indemnity plans and preferred provider organizations and 7% of HMOs cover no contraceptive method beyond sterilization.

how_it_helps.text: A group health plan or insurer that covers other outpatient prescription drugs or devices could no longer exclude or restrict FDA-approved prescription contraceptive drugs or devices.
Plans would have to cover outpatient contraceptive services — consultations, exams, and related medical care — if they cover other outpatient professional services.
Insurers could not deny or drop enrollment because of a person's use or potential use of contraception, and could not pay enrollees rebates to accept weaker protections.
Doctors could not have their reimbursement reduced, or be offered incentives, for prescribing contraceptives or for withholding them from patients.
Any deductibles, copays, or other limits on contraceptives could be no greater than what the plan applies to comparable drugs, devices, or outpatient services.
The rules would apply to individual-market coverage as well as group plans, and state laws providing stronger protections would not be preempted.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor group health plans would bear the added cost of covering contraception, which would be spread through premiums across enrollees. Insurers and employers would also face new compliance and notice requirements.

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises costs for insurers and employers, which would flow through premiums paid by all enrollees; a benefit mandate shifts the bill for one group of enrollees onto the whole risk pool rather than onto the federal budget.
The requirement is an equity rule, not a full coverage mandate: a plan that covers no outpatient prescription drugs or services at all would not be required to add contraceptive coverage.
Contraceptive-coverage mandates drew objection from some religious employers and institutions that objected to covering contraception on moral grounds; this bill contained no exemption for them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: women whose plans already cover other prescriptions would no longer pay full price for contraception, which the bill's own findings link to unintended pregnancy, higher infant mortality, and lower birth weights. The cost is real but limited by design — cost-sharing on contraceptives can be no higher than for comparable drugs, and the mandate only reaches plans that already cover other prescriptions. The unresolved objection is the absence of a religious exemption, which is why similar mandates have often been modified.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees, which passed it down to subcommittees in the spring of 2001, and it sat there with no markup, no hearing, and no vote until Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Greenwood (R-PA) introduced the Equity in Prescription Insurance and Contraceptive Coverage Act of 2001 on March 20, 2001.
The bill was referred to two committees, Education and the Workforce and Energy and Commerce, the standard practice for a bill touching both employee benefits and health insurance.
It attracted 144 cosponsors in the House: 129 of 208 Democrats, 14 of 223 Republicans, and the chamber's sole Independent.
In April 2001 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and in May 2001 to the Education and the Workforce Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a markup or a vote in either committee or on the House floor, and died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers that sponsor health plans are better off, since they never had to add contraceptive coverage or absorb the mandate's cost. The bill's cosponsors and the women it would have covered got nothing from this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was a Republican and it drew 14 Republican and 129 Democratic cosponsors, but both committees that held it were controlled by Republicans and it never reached a vote, so the party split shows up in who decided its fate rather than in any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have barred insurers from excluding prescription contraceptives from plans that cover other prescriptions, forcing them to add a benefit and its cost. Excluding contraceptive coverage was already the norm for many plans, so the mandate targeted an existing practice that saved insurers money at enrollees' expense.
Group plans, including self-insured plans governed by ERISA, would have had to cover contraception and send notice of the change. The cost would show up in premiums and benefits budgets.

Requiring plans that cover other prescriptions to cover FDA-approved contraceptives would have expanded the insured market for those drugs and devices. Their gain runs alongside the public benefit of affordable contraception.
